subtitle: Recognize and learn from cultural patterns without judging them by your own standard, and turn that recognition into practical, properly reviewed changes in DHS decisions.
audience: For DHS and DSD supervisors, policy and program staff, case managers, HR partners and communications staff who make or shape decisions affecting diverse communities. The Minimization course in this series is helpful background but not required.

lessons.title: Naming Acceptance: seeing patterns of difference and commonality
objectives: Describe Acceptance as the first intercultural mindset on the Intercultural Development Continuum.
Distinguish recognizing a cultural difference from agreeing with it or judging it.
Explain the gap the continuum names between recognizing difference and being able to adapt to it.
Identify the ethical challenge that can arise when several cultural approaches all make sense.
lessons.teaching:
This is the fourth course in the program's six-part series on the Intercultural Development Continuum. The continuum, published by IDI, LLC, moves from the monocultural mindsets of Denial and Polarization, through the transitional orientation of Minimization, to the intercultural mindsets of Acceptance and Adaptation. The program's series closes with Integration, drawn from Milton Bennett's earlier Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity. Acceptance is where attention shifts from what people share to how culture shapes what they do, while commonality stays in view.

The continuum describes Acceptance as an orientation in which people recognize and appreciate patterns of cultural difference and commonality in their own and other cultures. Two parts of that description matter. First, it includes one's own culture: in Acceptance, people start to see their own habits of communication, decision-making and respect as cultural patterns, not as the neutral baseline. Second, it describes curiosity. People with this orientation want to learn how a pattern of behavior makes sense within a different cultural community, rather than treating it as a strange exception to a normal rule. Bennett describes this as experiencing others as equally complex but different in form.

Acceptance does not mean agreeing with everything. Bennett is explicit that accepting the reality of a cultural difference is not the same as approving of it; a difference can still be judged negatively. What changes is how the judgment is made. Instead of measuring others against one's own cultural standard without noticing, a person in Acceptance tries first to understand the practice in its own context. In public service this matters, because staff work within laws, rules and safety standards that do apply to everyone. Acceptance helps people see what a practice means before deciding what the rule requires.

The continuum also names two limits. People in Acceptance are curious and appreciative but may not yet be fully able to adapt their own behavior to cultural difference. Knowing that a family makes decisions together is not the same as knowing how to run a planning meeting that works for them. And because people in Acceptance can see the value in many approaches, choosing one can be hard, which can show up as hesitation when a decision must be made across cultural groups. As in the whole series, this course uses the continuum as shared vocabulary. It does not administer the Intercultural Development Inventory or guess anyone's result; only a licensed Qualified Administrator can do that.
lessons.keyPoint: Acceptance means recognizing and being curious about cultural patterns, including your own, without assuming they must match yours. Recognition is not the same as agreement, and it is not yet the ability to adapt.
lessons.example: Fictional case: In a county partnership meeting, Megan, a DSD policy analyst, hears a Tribal social services director, Darrell, explain that some families in his community prefer that initial conversations about services happen through a respected relative before any formal meeting with the state. Megan is genuinely curious and asks thoughtful questions about why. Afterward, her team drafts an outreach plan. Megan realizes the plan still begins with a letter from the state inviting the person to a scheduled meeting. She understood the practice, but she is not sure what to change or whether she is allowed to change it.
lessons.question: What is the most useful next step for Megan?
choices: Rewrite the outreach plan herself around what she heard, since she now understands the community's practice.
Leave the plan as is, since her curiosity was respectful and the letter meets the requirement.

Bring the gap to her team and ask how to engage Darrell and the Tribal partner on options, routing any government-to-government questions through the department's Tribal relations and consultation process.
feedback: Understanding one conversation is not enough to redesign a plan for a sovereign nation's members. Acting alone risks replacing one assumption with another.
Curiosity without follow-through is the gap this lesson names. The requirement may be met, but the plan still may not reach the people it is meant for.
This is the strongest response. Megan names the gap between recognizing and adapting, involves her team and the partner, and respects formal Tribal consultation channels.
lessons.reflection: Think of a time you felt genuinely curious about a difference at work. What did you do with that curiosity afterward, and what, if anything, changed in your practice?
lessons.action: Choose one cultural pattern you have learned about through your work. Write down one question you still have about how it would affect a specific process you are responsible for, and identify who could help you answer it.

check.question: In Bennett's description of Acceptance, what is the relationship between accepting a cultural difference and agreeing with it?
check.correct: They are different: a person can recognize and understand a difference in context and still judge it negatively.
wrong: They are the same: accepting a difference means approving of it.
Acceptance means no longer making any judgments at all.
check.feedback: Acceptance changes how judgments are made, not whether they are made. The person first seeks to understand the practice in its own context instead of measuring it against an unnoticed personal standard. Judgment remains necessary, especially where laws and safety standards apply.

lessons.title: Noticing Acceptance in a team: curiosity without changed defaults
objectives: Identify signs that a team recognizes cultural difference but has not yet built it into its default practice.
Compare learning activities that increase curiosity with practice changes that affect decisions.
Explain why a team's knowledge about communities can remain separate from its decisions.
Draft a way to link what a team has learned to a specific process or decision point.
lessons.teaching:
A team in an Acceptance pattern often looks healthy from the outside. People are interested in the communities they serve. They attend cultural learning events, invite speakers, read community material and talk respectfully about difference. They can explain why a practice makes sense in context. What is often missing is the connection between that knowledge and the team's defaults. The intake script, the service planning template, the hiring panel questions and the timeline for public comment may look exactly as they did before the learning began.

This gap has understandable causes. Learning is voluntary and energizing; changing a process takes authority, time and coordination with other units. Staff may worry that adapting to one group means treating people unequally, or that there is no clear rule permitting the change. Others may see many valid approaches and hesitate to pick one, which the continuum names as a real challenge of Acceptance. The result can be a team that is sincere, informed and still producing the same results for the same people.

Some signs to watch for in DHS and DSD work: cultural learning shows up in presentations but not in the equity analysis for a decision. Community partners are thanked for their insight but rarely see how it changed anything. Staff know that certain families prefer in-person conversation, but the only outreach channel is a mailed notice. Interpreters are available, but meetings are still scheduled at times and in formats set without asking the family. A team may also describe itself as "culturally aware" as though awareness were the outcome, rather than the starting point for better service.

To move from noticing to linking, pick a specific decision point and ask: what do we now know about the people affected that we did not know before, and where in this process does it change what we do? The DHS Equity Policy expects authentic, ongoing community engagement and use of the Equity Analysis Toolkit for decisions with lasting impact. The toolkit's questions about who is affected, how partners were engaged, and what barriers exist are a practical bridge from a team's curiosity to its choices. The aim is not to adapt everything at once. It is to make sure that learning shows up somewhere concrete, and that partners can see the difference their input made.
lessons.keyPoint: A team can be curious and knowledgeable about difference while its forms, meetings and timelines stay the same. Link learning to a specific decision point so it changes practice.
lessons.example: Fictional case: A DSD unit held a well-attended series of lunch sessions with speakers from East African, Latino and Hmong community organizations. Staff describe the sessions as eye-opening. Six months later, Jae, a program specialist, is updating the unit's public input process for a proposed service rate change. The process still offers a single online comment form in English, open for thirty days, with a webinar during the workday. Jae remembers a speaker explaining that many people in her community learn about changes through community radio and trusted organizations.
lessons.question: What should Jae do?
choices: Propose that the unit revisit the input process with the Equity Analysis Toolkit, adding options suggested by partners, such as working with trusted organizations and offering translated and spoken ways to comment, within the rules that govern the comment period.
Send the lunch speakers a link to the online form and ask them to share it.
Assume the comment period rules make any change impossible and keep the existing process.
feedback: This is the strongest response. Jae links what the unit learned to a specific process, uses the department's method, and respects the formal rules for public comment while expanding how people can participate.
Sharing a link is a small step, but it asks partners to push the same inaccessible form and does not change the unit's default.
Rules about a comment period rarely dictate only one way to participate. Assuming no change is possible without checking leaves the unit's learning unused.
lessons.reflection: What is one thing your team has learned about the people you serve in the past year? Where, if anywhere, can you see it in how the team actually works?
lessons.action: Pick one process your team owns. Write one sentence naming something the team has learned about the people it affects, and one sentence naming where in the process that learning could change a step. Share it with your supervisor or team.

check.question: Which sign best suggests a team is recognizing difference but not yet adapting to it?
check.correct: Staff can explain why communities' practices make sense, but the team's forms, outreach and meeting formats have not changed.
wrong: Staff dismiss cultural differences as unimportant.
Staff say the team's way of doing things is better than other ways.
check.feedback: Dismissing difference or ranking cultures points to earlier orientations on the continuum. The Acceptance pattern is recognition and curiosity that has not yet reached practice. The next step is linking knowledge to specific decision points.

lessons.title: Finding your own Acceptance honestly
objectives: Identify signs in your own work of curiosity that has not yet translated into changed behavior.
Distinguish thoughtful openness from hesitation that avoids making a needed decision.
Explain how to make a decision across cultural perspectives that is grounded in context rather than one's own cultural standard.
Plan one specific behavior to practice in a real work situation.
lessons.teaching:
Many people who have worked in diverse settings will recognize parts of Acceptance in themselves. You enjoy learning how others see the world. You can explain why a practice that once puzzled you makes sense. You notice your own cultural habits more than you used to. These are real achievements. The honest question is what you do with them when a decision is on the table, and this lesson offers three places to look.

First, look for curiosity without follow-through. Do you ask good questions in meetings with partners, then write the same kind of plan you always write? Do you know that a person you serve prefers to include family in decisions, yet schedule the meeting in a way that makes that hard? These are not moral failures. They are signs that knowing about a difference has not yet become knowing how to work with it.

Second, look for hesitation that feels like respect. Because people in Acceptance can see the sense in many approaches, choosing one can feel like disrespecting the others. The continuum names this as a genuine challenge. In public service, though, not deciding is also a decision, and it often defaults to the existing process. Bennett describes the developmental task here as finding a basis for judgment that is not ethnocentric: first understanding each perspective in its own context, then making and owning a commitment. For DHS staff, that commitment is shaped by law, rule and program requirements, such as person-centered planning expectations under Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D or protections in the Positive Supports Rule. Understanding context helps you apply those requirements well; it does not replace them.

Third, look at whose perspective you are curious about. It is common to be very curious about communities that feel interesting and less curious about colleagues whose styles simply irritate you, including people from your own background. Acceptance includes seeing your own group's variety and your own culture as one pattern among many.

As with every course in this series, this reflection is private and practical. It is not a way to place yourself on the continuum or to assign yourself a stage. If you want a formal view of your orientation, the Intercultural Development Inventory is available only through a licensed Qualified Administrator, with a debrief. What you can do this week is pick a specific behavior, practice it, and ask for feedback.
lessons.keyPoint: Honest reflection on Acceptance asks what you do with your curiosity: whether it reaches your decisions, and whether respect for many views has turned into avoiding a needed choice.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Rosa, a DSD policy consultant, is drafting guidance on how lead agencies should involve families in support planning. Advisers have described very different preferences: some families want the person served to lead with minimal family role, others expect elders to be central, and some disabled self-advocates want firm protection of the person's own voice. Rosa sees merit in all of it. The draft is two weeks late because she keeps revising to avoid favoring any view.
lessons.question: What is the most useful way for Rosa to move forward?
choices: Keep revising until every adviser is fully satisfied with the language.

Ground the guidance in the person's own choice about who is involved, as person-centered requirements expect, explain how planners can support different family roles within that, and take the draft to her supervisor and legal or policy reviewers.
Pick the approach that matches how her own family makes decisions, since she understands it best.
feedback: Seeking full agreement from every perspective can become the hesitation this lesson describes. The guidance is still needed, and delay usually keeps the old default in place.

This is the strongest response. Rosa makes a grounded decision anchored in the requirements that protect the person's choice, keeps room for varied family roles, and uses formal review rather than deciding alone.
Choosing by one's own cultural standard is the ethnocentric basis for judgment that Acceptance moves away from, even when it is unintentional.
lessons.reflection: Is there a decision at work you have been putting off because several perspectives all seem reasonable? What would a grounded, explainable choice look like?
lessons.action: Choose one behavior to practice this week, such as asking a person served who they want involved before scheduling a meeting. Afterward, note what happened and what you would adjust next time.

check.question: What does Bennett describe as the developmental task for someone in Acceptance facing a decision across cultural perspectives?
check.correct: Understanding each perspective in context and then making and owning an ethical commitment that is not simply based on one's own cultural standard.
wrong: Avoiding decisions until every cultural group agrees.
Treating all practices as equally acceptable so no judgment is needed.
check.feedback: Acceptance can drift into paralysis or into the idea that anything goes. Bennett's framing asks for both: understand context first, then commit. In DHS work, that commitment also sits inside laws, rules and program requirements that the responsible offices interpret.

lessons.title: From recognizing to adapting: applying Acceptance to DHS decisions
objectives: Explain what separates Acceptance from Adaptation on the continuum.
Plan how to turn a recognized cultural difference into a specific change in a DHS or DSD decision.
Compare adapting a process with lowering a standard or making an unofficial exception.
Identify when a formal office, such as EOAD, the ADA coordinator, legal counsel or Tribal consultation, must be involved.
lessons.teaching:
The continuum describes Adaptation as the orientation in which people can shift perspective and adjust behavior in culturally appropriate and authentic ways. Acceptance builds the recognition; Adaptation builds the capacity to act. The bridge between them is practice: using what you understand in real situations, getting feedback and adjusting. The next course in this series explores Adaptation in depth. This lesson focuses on the first steps across that bridge in everyday department decisions.

A useful sequence has four moves. Recognize: name the cultural pattern that is relevant, including your own and the institution's. Understand: learn, from the people affected and from partners, how the pattern makes sense and what it means for this decision. Ask what the purpose requires: separate the legitimate standard, such as eligibility criteria, safety requirements or accuracy, from the method that has always been used to meet it. Adapt the method: change the channel, timing, format, participants or sequence so that more people can meet the same standard. This is not lowering the bar. A planning meeting held with the family members the person chooses, at a time they can attend, with a qualified interpreter, still has to produce a plan that meets program requirements.

Adapting also has limits that matter in a public agency. Staff should not make private exceptions to rules because they understand a community well. Changes to policy go through the responsible policy and legal review. Questions involving Tribal nations go through government-to-government consultation. Accommodation for disability goes through the ADA coordinator or the accommodation process. Concerns about discrimination go to EOAD. Acceptance helps you notice when those channels are needed; it does not replace them.

Leaders and supervisors can make adaptation easier. Build questions about cultural patterns into the Equity Analysis Toolkit discussions your unit already holds. Give staff permission to propose alternative methods that meet the same standard, with a clear route for approval. Close the loop with community partners by telling them what changed as a result of their input and what did not, and why. And treat adaptation as a skill that grows with practice, not a trait someone has or lacks. No one on the team should be asked to disclose their own cultural background or identity to justify a change; the evidence comes from the people affected and the decision's results.
lessons.keyPoint: Acceptance recognizes difference; Adaptation acts on it. Separate the standard from the method, adapt the method with the people affected, and use formal channels for policy, Tribal, accommodation and discrimination questions.
lessons.example: Fictional case: A DSD team is revising how people learn they may be eligible for a new self-directed service option. Samira, the team lead, has heard from a Karen community organization and a Deaf community advisory group that the planned written notice and phone line will not reach many people. Her team understands why. Now they must decide what to do before the rollout date. Ben suggests adding plain-language translated notices and a video in American Sign Language, co-produced with the advisory group, and asking partner organizations to host information sessions. Chloe worries that doing this for some groups is unequal treatment.
lessons.question: How should Samira respond to Chloe's concern?
choices: Agree with Chloe and keep one written notice for everyone so treatment is identical.
Approve Ben's plan immediately and skip review, since the team clearly understands the communities involved.

Explain that the eligibility standard stays the same for everyone while the methods of reaching people widen, and move the plan through the unit's equity analysis and communications review, including the accessibility and language access requirements that apply.
feedback: Identical notices do not give people an equal chance to learn about the option. This returns to Minimization at the moment of decision.
The plan is promising, but skipping review risks errors in translation, accessibility or legal requirements, and removes accountability for the decision.
This is the strongest response. Samira separates the standard from the method, addresses Chloe's fairness concern directly, and adapts through the department's normal review rather than informally.
lessons.reflection: Think of a recent decision where you understood a relevant cultural difference. What was the standard, what was the method, and could the method have changed while the standard stayed the same?
lessons.action: Take one upcoming decision in your work and write two lines: the standard that must stay the same, and one method that could be adapted with the people affected. Identify which office, if any, would need to approve the change.

check.question: What most clearly distinguishes Adaptation from Acceptance on the Intercultural Development Continuum?
check.correct: Adaptation includes the ability to shift perspective and adjust behavior in culturally appropriate ways, not only to recognize and appreciate differences.
wrong: Adaptation means giving up one's own cultural identity.
Adaptation means applying exactly the same approach to every group.
check.feedback: Adaptation adds the capacity to act across cultural difference in ways that are authentic and appropriate. It does not require losing one's own identity, and it moves away from, not toward, a single identical approach.

cards.back: On the Intercultural Development Continuum, an intercultural mindset in which people recognize and appreciate patterns of cultural difference and commonality in their own and other cultures.
Accepting that a cultural difference is real and makes sense in context does not mean approving of it. Judgment remains, but it is based on context rather than one's own unexamined standard.
People in Acceptance may understand a difference well yet not know how to adjust their own behavior or process in response.
The requirement that must stay the same, such as eligibility or safety, and the way it is met, such as channel, format, timing or participants, which can often be adapted.
The next orientation on the continuum: the ability to shift perspective and adjust behavior in culturally appropriate and authentic ways.

aid.heading: Link learning to a decision
items: Name what the team has learned about the people this decision affects.
Identify the exact step in the process where that learning could change something.
Use the Equity Analysis Toolkit questions on who is affected and how partners were engaged.
Tell partners what changed because of their input, and what did not and why.

aid.heading: Decide across perspectives
items: Understand each perspective in its own context before judging.
Separate the standard that must stay the same from the method that could change.
Make and explain a decision instead of waiting for full agreement.
Anchor decisions in the person's own choices and applicable law and rules.

aid.heading: Use formal channels
items: Policy changes go through policy and legal review.
Questions involving Tribal nations go through government-to-government consultation.
Disability accommodation goes through the ADA coordinator or accommodation process.
Discrimination concerns go to EOAD; never make private exceptions to rules.
